News Release
Virtual power plant capacity expands 25.9% year-over-year to reach 47.2 GW
VPP growth outpaces deployments, programs and offtakers

18 November 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

The virtual power plant (VPP) market grew rapidly over the last year, reaching 47.2 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity, according to a new report from Wood Mackenzie.
 
The report, “2026 North America virtual power plant market report”, finds that the VPP market deepened more than it broadened this year, as capacity expanded 25.9%, outpacing growth in the number of company deployments, unique offtakers, and market and utility programs monetized, which each expanded less than 15%.
“Escalating turbine costs, affordability concerns and slow supply response to large loads are driving more interest in VPPs,” said Elham Akhavan, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie.
Akhavan noted that with heavy-turbine capex expanding more than 80% since 2020, BESS VPPs now win on cost per kW in 2026. Distributed BESS retained its position as the most cost-effective in this time frame.
Market maturation accelerates in some sectors
The largest jump in VPP wholesale market capacity recorded in the residential market, with 155% expansion year-over-year.
"Residential’s share of wholesale-market VPP capacity more than doubled, reflecting opt-out enrollment and retailer-led battery growth," said Max Issokson, senior research analyst, Wood Mackenzie.
Storage and EV penetration relative to thermostats experienced impressive growth as well, displaying a 19.7% YOY growth and outpacing 2025’s growth. The only portion that contracted was economic participants in the market, with growth shrinking 13.5% YOY.
Evolving markets
PJM and ERCOT remain the regions with the greatest utility commitments to data center capacity, also have the greatest disclosed VPP offtake capacity.
Emerging markets such as MISO, as well as activity in Arizona, Illinois and Virginia are demonstrating opportunity for more growth.
Summer capacity prices rose significantly in MISO this year, from $30 to $384-424/MW-day, but aggregation rules still limit growth.
“Arizona, Virginia and Illinois are building new programs that may increase capacity,” said Akhavan. “California has been a strong market in the past, but its future growth depends on SB 913 versus one-off DSGS funding.”
Data centers and the competitive frontier
The 2026 report identifies a new signal in the market, with VPP providers disclosing a 1 GW pipeline of capacity specifically targeting data center load, a category that did not appear in last year's scorecard, demonstrating that VPPs are increasingly positioned as a direct response to the infrastructure demands. 
Competition among commercial and industrial aggregators is tightening as well, with battery ownership and optimization emerging as key points of differentiation.
“Financiers are divided on how to account for VPP revenue, with some pricing it directly into storage leases, while others pass it through to customers as a bill credit or direct incentive,” said Akhavan. “How that revenue is treated is becoming a defining competitive variable.
At the same time, the report cautions that deployed storage does not automatically translate into VPP capacity. Opt-out enrollment has demonstrated it can shift capacity overnight, while opt-in models and data access barriers continue to constrain growth.
